# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

SPL is a pipeline: each command receives the results of the previous one and passes its output on, like a Unix pipe. Most investigations use the same dozen commands — search and where to filter, stats and timechart to aggregate, eval and rex to create fields, lookup to enrich, and join or transaction to combine related events. Knowing what each does, and in which order to use them, makes searches fast and correct.  
In this lab you load a one-hour incident (INC-9120) across four indexes and build SPL step by step on it: filtering, aggregating by status and backend, time charts of errors, derived fields, regex extraction of the backend and API, enrichment with host and owner lookups, and correlation of web and application events with join and transaction. Every result has an exact expected value so you can check your searches.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You can turn a question into a correct SPL pipeline and prove the answer with numbers. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You will choose the right command — filter early, aggregate late, enrich before you report. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: The INC-9120 dataset and lookups are reused in Lab 2 for the full investigation. |

| YOUR MISSION: Load the data and build the searches with stats, timechart, eval, rex, lookup, join and transaction. You have 28 minutes for the core tasks. |

*Figure: Day 3 Lab 1 — Starting Environment: Splunk Enterprise with No d3\_\* Indexes; INC-9120 Generator and Load Script*

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

An SPL search is a pipeline. The first part retrieves events; every \| passes results to the next command.  
*Figure: SPL Pipeline — index=… sourcetype=… host=… earliest/latest (retrieve) \| where / search (filter) \| eval / rex / lookup (enrich) \| stats / timechart (aggregate) \| sort / table (present)*

| Command | Type | What It Does | Example in This Lab |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| search / where | Filter | search: terms and field=value; where: eval expressions (rt \> 2\) | index=d3\_web status=502 \| where rt \< 0.01 |
| stats / timechart | Aggregate | Group and calculate; timechart groups by time buckets | stats count avg(rt) perc95(rt) by upstream |
| eval / rex / lookup | Create / enrich fields | Calculate, extract with regex, add fields from a CSV | rex "upstream=(?\<backend\>app-\\d+)" \| lookup host\_inventory.csv … |
| join / transaction | Correlate | join: combine with a subsearch by field; transaction: group events into one | transaction req\_id startswith=… endswith=… |

*Figure: Filter Early, Aggregate Late — Retrieval Terms (index, sourcetype, host, time) Cut the Data at the Indexers Before Any Pipeline Command Runs*

## 1.4  Learning Objectives

* Explain the SPL search pipeline and the role of index, sourcetype, host and time range  
* Filter with search and where  
* Aggregate with stats and timechart  
* Create fields with eval and extract fields with rex  
* Enrich events with lookup  
* Correlate events with join and transaction and explain when to use each

## 1.5  What You Will NOT Do

| 🚫  Hard Stops — Absolute Prohibitions for This Lab |
| :---- |
| ✗  NEVER run d3 searches without the explicit earliest/latest window — the data is from 22 Oct 2026, not "now" |
| ✗  NEVER use join or transaction where stats by a common field gives the same answer — they are expensive |
| ✗  NEVER overwrite lookup files that other teams use — the lab lookups have their own names |
| ✗  NEVER delete indexes you did not create |
| ✗  NEVER rely on rex results without checking a few raw events first |

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Retrieval Terms vs Pipeline Commands

Everything before the first pipe is evaluated by the indexers while reading data: index, sourcetype, host, source, time range and search terms. The narrower this part is, the less data the rest of the pipeline has to process. Commands after the pipe work on the retrieved events (streaming commands such as eval, rex, where, lookup) or on the whole result set (transforming commands such as stats, timechart, transaction). A good search therefore filters early, enriches only what it needs, and aggregates last.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| During an incident the same questions come back again and again: how many, how fast, since when, which host, which team. A few well-built searches answer all of them. |
|  |
| stats can replace most join and transaction use cases at a fraction of the cost: stats values(…) by req\_id combines events from several sources without subsearch limits. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: search vs where

search (and the terms before the first pipe) matches terms and field=value pairs, with wildcards, and is case-insensitive for values. where evaluates an eval expression — numeric comparisons between fields, functions like like(), match(), isnull() — and is case-sensitive. Use search-style terms to cut data early, and where for calculations and comparisons that search cannot express.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake With SPL |
| :---- |
| An engineer writes index=\* \| where status=502 \| … over All time to find errors — the search reads every event in every index, then throws almost all of them away. |
|  |
| REASON: where is a pipeline command; it runs only after all events were retrieved. |
|  |
| YOU MUST put index, sourcetype, host, time range and simple field=value terms before the first pipe, and use where only for what search terms cannot do. |

## 3.3  join vs transaction vs stats

| Command | Best For | Cost / Limits | Alternative |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| join | Adding fields from a different search by a key | Subsearch limits (rows, time); runs twice | stats values() by key over both indexes |
| transaction | Grouping related events with start/end, duration, eventcount | Memory-heavy; needs time order | stats min(\_time) max(\_time) by key |
| stats | Counting and calculating per group | Cheap, distributable | — |
| lookup | Static enrichment (inventory, owners) | CSV size | KV store lookups for large tables |

| 📝  How to Decide Which Correlation Command to Use |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Do I need the events grouped with their duration and order, or just combined numbers per key?" For numbers per key use stats. For start/end grouping with duration use transaction, ideally on few events. For adding a few fields from another search use join (or better a lookup if the data is static). Always test the faster option first. |

# 4\. LAB TASKS

*Figure: Day 3 Lab 1 — Four-Task SPL Fundamentals SOP Workflow*  
*Figure: Expected Result — 85 × 502 All via app-02, p95 1.65 s on app-02, 5xx Only at 10:30–10:39, Backend app-02 → dc2 → commerce-oncall, App Duration Matches Web rt*

| TASK 1 — PIPELINE: search, where and the First Statistics |
| :---- |

| 1 | Build the Search Pipeline with search, where and stats*Splunk SPL Fundamentals SOP — Day 3 — Lab 1* | ⏱ 6 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

The first searches retrieve one index for the incident window, count by status, and use where for a numeric comparison that would be awkward as a search term. Watch the event counts change as each command is added.

| ⌨  Task 1 — Search & Reporting (one search per line) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: Retrieve and count by status |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" \| stats count by status |
|  |
| \# Step 2: The 502s — how fast did they fail? (where compares numbers) |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" status=502 \| where rt \< 0.01 \| stats count |
|  |
| \# Step 3: Very slow requests (more than 2 s) — which backend? |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" \| where rt \> 2 \| stats count by upstream |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: 200 → 1775 · 201 → 493 · 404 → 47 · 502 → 85![][image3] |
| Step 2: 85   (every 502 failed in under 10 ms — the backend refused the connection) ![][image4] |
| Step 3: app-02:8080 → 25 ![][image5] |
| **1.A  Why is status=502 written before the first pipe but rt \< 0.01 after it, with where?**  Answer: `status=502` is a simple field-value filter that can be applied during retrieval before the first pipe. `where rt < 0.01` performs a numeric comparison using an eval expression, so it is applied after retrieving the events.  |
| **1.B  What do "fast 502s" tell you about the failure mode, compared with slow 504s?**  Answer: Fast 502s indicate that the backend refused the connection or was unavailable, causing an immediate failure. Slow 504s indicate that the request waited for the backend until a timeout occurred.  |

# 

| TASK 2 — AGGREGATE: stats, timechart and eval |
| :---- |

| 2 | Aggregate with stats and timechart and Derive Fields with eval*Splunk SPL Fundamentals SOP — Day 3 — Lab 1* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

stats calculates per group, timechart per time bucket, and eval creates new fields from existing ones. Together they show which backend was slow, when errors happened, and how requests split into status classes.

| ⌨  Task 2 — stats, timechart, eval |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: Per backend: requests, average and p95 response time |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" \| stats count avg(rt) AS avg\_rt perc95(rt) AS p95\_rt by upstream \| eval avg\_rt=round(avg\_rt,3), p95\_rt=round(p95\_rt,2) |
|  |
| \# Step 2: eval — status class and a slow flag |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" \| eval class=floor(status/100)."xx" \| stats count by class |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" \| eval slow=if(rt\>1,1,0) \| stats sum(slow) AS slow\_requests by upstream |
|  |
| \# Step 3: timechart — 5xx per 5 minutes next to the total |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" \| timechart span=5m count(eval(status\>=500)) AS errors\_5xx count AS total |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: app-01:8080 800 0.094 ≈0.30 · app-02:8080 800 0.243 ≈1.65 · app-03:8080 800 0.088 ≈0.30 ![][image6] |
| Step 2: 2xx 2268 · 4xx 47 · 5xx 85 ![][image7]   app-01:8080 0 · app-02:8080 75 · app-03:8080 0 ![][image8] |
| Step 3: total 200 in every 5-minute bucket; errors\_5xx 0 except 10:30 → 54 and 10:35 → 31![][image9] |
| **2.A  Record avg and p95 for app-02 and the others. Why is p95 more useful than the average here?**  Answer: app-01: Average 0.094 s, P95 0.30 s.app-02: Average 0.243 s, P95 1.65 s.app-03: Average 0.088 s, P95 0.30 s. P95 is more useful because it highlights slow response times experienced by the slowest 5% of requests, whereas the average can hide latency spikes. |
| **2.B  The slow requests (75) and the 502s (85) are both on app-02. From the timechart, which came first?**  Answer: The slow requests came first, beginning around 10:24. The 502 errors occurred later, starting at 10:30. This indicates that performance degradation preceded the backend failures. |

# 

| TASK 3 — EXTRACT & ENRICH: rex and lookup |
| :---- |

| 3 | Extract Fields with rex and Enrich Results with lookup*Splunk SPL Fundamentals SOP — Day 3 — Lab 1* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

rex extracts new fields with a regular expression (named groups). lookup adds fields from a CSV table by a matching key. You extract the backend host and the API name, then enrich the 502s with data centre, service and the owning on-call team.

| ⌨  Task 3 — rex and lookup |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: rex — backend name without the port, and API name from the path |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" \| rex "upstream=(?\<backend\>app-\\d+):(?\<port\>\\d+)" \| stats count by backend, port |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" \| rex field=uri\_path "^/api/(?\<api\>\[a-z\]+)" \| stats count by api |
|  |
| \# Step 2: lookup — data centre and service of the backend, then the owner of the service |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" status=502 \| rex "upstream=(?\<backend\>app-\\d+)" |
| \| lookup host\_inventory.csv host AS backend OUTPUT datacenter service |
| \| lookup service\_owners.csv service OUTPUT team oncall |
| \| stats count by backend, datacenter, service, team, oncall |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: app-01 8080 800 · app-02 8080 800 · app-03 8080 800![][image10] |
|         cart 611 · orders 505 · products 1098   (the 186 /health requests have no api value)![][image11] |
| Step 2: app-02  dc2  shop-api  commerce  commerce-oncall  85 ![][image12] |
| **3.A  Why does the second lookup work although the events never contained a service field?**  Answer: The first lookup adds the `service` field using the backend hostname as the matching key. The second lookup uses this newly added `service` field to retrieve the corresponding team and on-call details.  |
| **3.B  Write a rex that extracts the request id number (100961 from req\_id=r-100961) into a field req\_num.**   Answer: \| rex field=req\_id "r-(?\<req\_num\>\\d+)"  |

| ⚠️  STOP CHECK — Your Lookups Must Return the Owner Before You Correlate |
| :---- |
| Before moving to Task 4, confirm Step 2 shows commerce-oncall. Task 4 correlates web and application events; Lab 2 uses the same lookups to route the incident. |
|  |
| If in doubt — run \| inputlookup service\_owners.csv and show your instructor. |

# 

| TASK 4 — CORRELATE: transaction and join |
| :---- |

| 4 | Correlate Events with transaction and join*Splunk SPL Fundamentals SOP — Day 3 — Lab 1* | ⏱ 8 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

transaction groups the START and END events of each request into one result with a duration. join adds the application duration to slow web requests through the shared req\_id. You compare both with the web response time.

| ⌨  Task 4 — transaction and join |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: transaction — application time per request, by host |
| index=d3\_app earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" (msg=START OR msg=END) |
| \| transaction req\_id startswith=eval(msg=="START") endswith=eval(msg=="END") maxspan=30s |
| \| stats count avg(duration) AS avg\_s max(duration) AS max\_s by host \| eval avg\_s=round(avg\_s,3) |
|  |
| \# Step 2: join — the first three slow web requests with the application duration |
| index=d3\_web earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" rt\>1 |
| \| join type=left req\_id \[search index=d3\_app earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" msg=END \| rename host AS app\_host \| fields req\_id duration\_ms app\_host\] |
| \| eval web\_ms=round(rt\*1000) \| sort \_time \| head 3 \| table \_time req\_id upstream app\_host web\_ms duration\_ms |
|  |
| \# Step 3: The same correlation with stats (no join) — compare the speed in the Job inspector |
| (index=d3\_web rt\>1) OR (index=d3\_app msg=END) earliest="10/22/2026:10:00:00" latest="10/22/2026:11:00:00" |
| \| stats values(rt) AS rt values(duration\_ms) AS app\_ms values(host) AS hosts by req\_id \| where isnotnull(rt) \| head 3 |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: app-01 800 0.091 0.347 · app-02 715 0.269 2.461 · app-03 800 0.085 0.347   (app-02: 85 requests never arrived)![][image13] |
| Step 2: 10:24:01 r-100961 app-02:8080 app-02 1637 1634 |
|         10:24:06 r-100964 app-02:8080 app-02 1726 1724 |
|         10:24:10 r-100967 app-02:8080 app-02 2038 2035![][image14] |
| Step 3: r-100961 1.637 1634 app-02 web-0x · r-100964 … · r-100967 …   (same numbers, one search)![][image15] |
| **4.A  Web rt and application duration differ by only \~3 ms. What does that say about where the time was spent?**  Answer: `transaction` groups related START and END events using the common request ID and calculates the time taken to complete each request. |
| **4.B  Compare the run times of Step 2 and Step 3 in the Job inspector. When would you still use join or transaction?**  Answer: `stats` aggregates events by a common request ID in one pipeline, making it more efficient and scalable. `join` uses a subsearch with row and time limits, which can affect performance and truncate results. |

# 

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Searches return 0 events | Time range not 22 Oct 2026 10:00–11:00, or wrong user time zone | Run with earliest=0 | Use the explicit earliest/latest; set Preferences → Time zone to Asia/Kolkata |
| Counts are doubled | load-day3.sh was run twice | stats count by source | Delete and recreate the d3\_\* indexes, load once |
| rt or upstream field missing | Sourcetype not access\_combined (no automatic key=value) | index=d3\_web \| head 1 \| table sourcetype rt upstream | Reload web files with \-sourcetype access\_combined |
| lookup: "could not find lookup table" | CSV not in the search app lookups folder | ls \$SPLUNK\_HOME/etc/apps/search/lookups | Copy the CSV files (sudo if needed); run searches in the Search app |
| transaction returns fewer transactions | maxspan too small, or START/END filter missing | Check duration distribution | Use maxspan=30s and (msg=START OR msg=END) |
| join returns empty app fields | Subsearch time range or field name mismatch | Run the subsearch alone | Same earliest/latest in the subsearch; field req\_id in both |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — The Pipeline |
| :---- |
| Without notes: classify search, where, eval, rex, lookup, stats, timechart, join and transaction as filter, enrich, aggregate or correlate. |
| Which belong before the first pipe? |
|  |
| Key answer to explore: retrieval terms first; streaming enrichment next; transforming aggregation last. |
| **Discussion 2 — What the Numbers Say** |
| Using only your Lab 1 results, describe INC-9120 in three sentences. |
| Which result made the cause obvious? |
|  |
| Key insight: all slow and failed requests share one backend (app-02); slowness preceded the 502s. |
| **Discussion 3 — join vs stats** |
| Why was the stats version of the correlation faster? |
| What are the subsearch limits that make join risky on large data? |
|  |
| Key answer: stats runs once and distributes; join runs a subsearch with row/time limits and can silently truncate. |
| **Discussion 4 — Lookups** |
| Which other lookups would help on-call engineers (CMDB, runbooks, change calendar)? |
| Who should own and update them? |
|  |
| Answer: inventory and ownership lookups turn a host name into a team and a runbook; they need an owner and automation. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| where for simple field=value filters | Looks like SQL | Slow searches | Put field=value before the first pipe |
| No time range | Default "Last 24 hours" | No results (historic data) or too much data | Explicit earliest/latest |
| transaction everywhere | Convenient duration field | Memory and time costs | stats min/max(\_time) by key |
| Unchecked rex | Regex "looks right" | Wrong or empty fields | Test on raw events; count results |
| Hard-coded owners in searches | Quick fix | Out-of-date routing | Use lookup tables with an owner |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — SPLUNK SPL FUNDAMENTALS COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Retrieve | index=… sourcetype=… host=… earliest=… latest=… | Before the first pipe |
| where | \| where rt \> 2 AND status\!=200 | Eval expressions |
| stats | \| stats count avg(x) perc95(x) by f | Group and calculate |
| timechart | \| timechart span=5m count(eval(status\>=500)) AS e | Per time bucket |
| eval | \| eval class=floor(status/100)."xx" | New fields |
| rex | \| rex "upstream=(?\<backend\>app-\\d+)" | Regex extraction |
| rex field | \| rex field=uri\_path "^/api/(?\<api\>\[a-z\]+)" | From a field |
| lookup | \| lookup file.csv key AS field OUTPUT a b | Enrich |
| inputlookup | \| inputlookup file.csv | Read a lookup |
| transaction | \| transaction id startswith=… endswith=… maxspan=30s | duration, eventcount |
| join | \| join type=left id \[search …\] | Subsearch (limits\!) |
| stats correlation | \| stats values(a) values(b) by id | Cheaper than join |
